procedural_history.impugned_order: Orders dated November 27, 1971 and December 22, 1971 of the Allahabad High Court in Applications Nos. A-112 and A-141 in Election Petition No. 5 of 1971 respectively. These orders relate to: 1) setting aside interrogatories served and striking out Issues 1 to 3; and 2) rejecting the application seeking permission to amend the election petition.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. An election petition (No. 5 of 1971) was filed by the appellant challenging the validity of the election of respondent No. 1.
2. The appellant served interrogatories on the respondent.
3. The High Court set aside the interrogatories and struck out Issues 1 to 3.
4. The appellant applied to amend the election petition, which was rejected by the High Court.
5. During the pendency of the appeal in the Supreme Court, the respondent filed an application before the High Court under rule 7, Order XI, C.P.C. praying that the interrogatories served on her may be set aside.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture:
1. The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the High Court's orders dated November 27, 1971 and December 22, 1971.
2. The respondent appealed against the order to the Supreme Court after obtaining special leave.
3. The respondent's appeal was withdrawn during the course of the hearing.
4. Civil Appeal No. 108 of 1972 is directed against the order setting aside the interrogatories served and the striking out of Issues 1 to 3.
5. Civil Appeal No. 109 of 1972 arises from the order rejecting the application seeking permission to amend the election petition.

issue.issue_text: Whether the trial court was justified in striking out the issues relating to corrupt practice.

facts: The trial court struck out the issues relating to corrupt practice.
The trial court's reasoning was that the facts stated in the election petition did not sufficiently disclose the alleged corrupt practice.
Specifically, the petition did not explicitly state that the respondent was a "candidate" at the time she allegedly obtained assistance from a government servant.
law: The Supreme Court established a distinction between the standard for pleading a corrupt practice and the standard for proving it.
While a corrupt practice must be strictly proven, the pleading itself should not be subjected to an overly strict construction.
If a pleading, on a reasonable construction, can sustain the action, the court should accept that construction and not frustrate the case on technical grounds.
A petition is not liable to be dismissed simply because full particulars of the corrupt practice are not set out initially.
application: The Court applied this legal principle to the facts of the case.
It acknowledged that the petition omitted the specific allegation that the respondent was a "candidate" when the assistance was obtained.
However, the Court found that this fact "flows as a necessary implication" from the other allegations made in the petition.

The Court emphasized that the purity of elections is essential to democracy and that a serious charge of corrupt practice should not be dismissed on a technicality if the core of the allegation is present in the pleadings.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the trial court was not justified in striking out the issues. It held that the allegations in the petition, when reasonably construed, were sufficient to disclose the corrupt practice, even if one ingredient was not explicitly stated but was a necessary implication of the other facts pleaded.

issue.issue_text: Whether the trial court was right in striking out the interrogatories.

facts: The appellant served 31 interrogatories on the respondent related to Issues 1, 2, and 3 in the case.
The respondent objected to these interrogatories, arguing they were "unreasonable, vexatious, oppressive, unnecessary and irrelevant".
The trial court struck out the interrogatories.
Interrogatories Nos. 24 to 30 had already been allowed and were not part of the Supreme Court's consideration.
law: The only questions that are relevant as interrogatories are those that relate to "any matters in question" in the suit.
Questions that may be relevant during cross-examination are not necessarily relevant as interrogatories.
To be permissible, interrogatories must touch the core of the allegations, not merely the fringe of the matter.
application: The Court analyzed the remaining interrogatories in two groups.
First, it found that Interrogatories Nos. 19 to 23 related to Issue No. 2 and were therefore correctly struck out.

Second, after carefully examining Interrogatories Nos. 1 to 18 and 31, the Court determined that none of them touched upon the "core of the allegations" related to the corrupt practice, which was the subject of Issue No. 1.
The Court characterized these interrogatories as only touching "the fringe of the matter," making them irrelevant under the established legal standard.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the trial court was right to strike out the interrogatories because they were not sufficiently relevant to the core matters in question in the suit, as required by law.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the trial court was justified in striking out the issues relating to corrupt practice.
appellant_arguments: The petition was not liable to be dismissed in limine simply because full particulars of the corrupt practice were not set out.
The petition contained all the necessary ingredients of the corrupt practice charge.
The petitioner should have been given an opportunity to amend the petition by giving better particulars.
The proposed amendments were merely clarificatory in nature and did not add new material facts, so they should have been allowed.
respondent_arguments: The relevant provisions of the Act precluded the appellant from proving his allegations as they were pleaded.
The allegations were too vague and elastic, failing to state the material facts, which was an intolerable position for the respondent.
The petition should be rejected in limine for failing to set out full particulars of the corrupt practice.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the trial court was right in striking out the interrogatories.
appellant_arguments: The interrogatories served on the respondent were proper and should have been allowed.
respondent_arguments: The interrogatories served by the appellant should be set aside, as requested in the application filed under Order XI, Rule 7, C.P.C.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A court must not refuse to inquire into a party's allegations or deny them an opportunity to prove their case merely because the pleadings were poorly drafted. It is the duty of the court to ascertain and implement the underlying juristic principle of a provision of law.
obiter: Rules of pleadings are intended as aids for a fair trial and for reaching a just decision.
An action at law should not be equated to a game of chess.
Provisions of law are not mere formulas to be observed as rituals.
Beneath the words of a provision of law, generally speaking, there lies a juristic principle.
The implications of the rule of law are manifold.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that an election petition should not be dismissed for technical defects in pleading if it contains all the essential ingredients of a corrupt practice charge. The primary duty of the court is to conduct a fair trial and reach a just decision, not to enforce pleading rules as rigid rituals that would prevent an inquiry into serious allegations.
legal_tests_applied: A petition is not liable to be dismissed in limine simply because full particulars of the corrupt practice alleged were not set out.
The court must assess whether the petition, taken as a whole, contains all the necessary ingredients of the corrupt practice charge, even if not perfectly articulated.
